6.80.m: Glorious Pārvatī said: / Ah, speak the glorification of Viṣṇu, the Lord, Master of the Universe, / having heard whose glorification, one is never born again in worldly existence.
Mahādeva said: / Listen, O beautiful one, I will declare the supreme glorification of Viṣṇu; / having heard it, one gains religious merit, and in the end attains liberation.
[To Nārada], devoted to divine vows, highly intelligent, dedicated to the yoga of meditation, / a refuge of all scriptures, possessing controlled senses, stainless,
invincible, highly fortunate, even to the gods along with Indra, / true to his promise, having conquered anger, steadfast in equanimity,
having reached supreme steadfastness in Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe, the refuge, affectionate toward devotees, / through actions of speech, mind, and body—
Bowing with his head to the earth before grandfather Bhīṣma, the scion of the Kurus, / who was calm and the abode of virtues, Yudhiṣṭhira asked this:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Some say highest is dharma, some say highest is wealth; / some praise generosity, and others assembly.
Some praise Sāṅkhya, others Yoga as supreme; / some praise knowledge, and some say highest is sacred tradition; / some [praise] proper meditation as supreme, others excellent detachment.
Others likewise consider ritual acts such as the Agniṣṭoma supreme; / some, viewing a clod of earth, a stone, and gold alike, consider knowledge of the self supreme.
Some [praise] moral restraints and religious observances, and excellent detachment; / some others, ascetics, [praise] compassion and non-violence.
Some men say purity is supreme, others the worship of gods; / and men bewildered by sinful acts fall into confusion in this matter.
You ought to tell me, O knower of dharma, O best of all who uphold the scriptures, / what among these is the highest duty to be undertaken by the great-souled.

Mahādeva said: / The sacred narrative between Bhīṣma and Yudhiṣṭhira that arose in the earthly realm, / that I shall relate for the welfare of all worlds. / Hearing these questions at that time, Bhīṣma spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bhīṣma said: / Let this most secret release from the cycle of rebirth be heard, / which ought to be heard by you and fully understood, O son of Dharma.
In this very regard, they cite this holy and ancient [narrative], / the dialogue between Puṇḍarīka and the great sage Nārada.
There was a brāhmaṇa named Puṇḍarīka, endowed with Vedic learning and of great intellect; / staying in the first stage of life, he was always obedient to his teachers,
with senses subdued and anger conquered, devoted to the twilight worship, / skilled in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and expert in the scriptures.
Having offered oblations to the fire morning and evening with kindling and pure offerings, / meditating upon Viṣṇu, the lord of the universe, he rightly worshipped the omnipresent Lord.
Devoted to austerity and recitation of the Vedas, like a son of Brahmā in bodily form, / he repeatedly worshipped his teacher with water, fuel, flowers, and the like.
Attentive to his mother and father, eating begged food, free from envy, / studying the science of Brahman, and devoted to breath control,
to that great-souled one, who saw all as his own self and was indifferent to saṃsāra, / there arose an intellect capable of carrying him across the ocean of worldly existence.
Having abandoned his mother and father, his brothers, benevolent relatives, / friends, maternal uncles, companions, kinsmen, and relations,
his home resembling Indra's, filled with wealth and grain, / and greatly valuable fields producing all kinds of crops,
like worthless blades of grass, that one of great fortitude, exceedingly joyful, / wandered across the delightful earth, living on herbs, roots, and fruits.
To the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the Gomatī and the Gaṇḍakī, / the Śatadru, the Payoṣṇī, the Sarayū, and the Sarasvatī,
Prayāga, the Narmadā, the great river Śoṇa, / Prabhāsa, the tīrthas of the Vindhya range, and those originating from the Himavat,
and those which are in the hermitages, in Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, and the rest, / and those in Kurukṣetra, and likewise at Govardhana and elsewhere—
to other sacred tīrthas, that great yogī of exceedingly great splendour, / thoroughly composed, wandered in accordance with time and rule.
Once, the self-controlled, steadfast ascetic, / the illustrious Puṇḍarīka, led by the force of past actions,
[went to] Śālagrāma, frequented by sages who know the truth and are rich in austerities, / a delightful abode of sages, renowned even in the Purāṇas,
adorned with disc [impressions] and the like, its rock-surfaces marked with discs, / delightful, solitary, expansive, and always pleasing to Viṣṇu.
Moreover, creatures there, marked with discs and of holy sight, / wander at will, beholding that holy tīrtha.
In that exceedingly holy sacred field of Śāligrāma, of great intellect / and steadfast vows, having bathed at Devahrada tīrtha and in the Sarasvatī,
at the Jātismaryā, the Cakratīrtha, and at places adjacent to the Cakra river, / as well as at other tīrthas, he wandered in that very place.
Then, by the majesty of the sacred field and the power of the tīrthas, / that noble-minded one attained serene clarity of mind right there.
With his soul purified by the tīrtha, the ascetic Puṇḍarīka / made his dwelling right there, wholly devoted to meditation and yoga.
Desiring spiritual accomplishment in that very place, having worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa / according to the rules declared in the scriptures, and with supreme devotion,
he dwelt alone for a long time, free from the pairs of opposites, with senses subdued, / eating herbs, roots, and fruits, contented, seeing all things equally.
By moral restraints, religious observances, and steady postures, / by breath controls, bathing in tīrthas, and continuous sensory withdrawals,
by concentrations, meditations, and absorptions, unwearied, / with impurities removed, he continually practiced yoga properly.
With Vedic and ancillary [chants], and with Purāṇic hymns as well, / he worshipped the Lord of all, and thereby attained purity.
Completely freed from attachment and aversion, the very embodiment of his own duty, / he worshipped God with his inner self directed towards Him.
The Lord Viṣṇu, whose eyes are wide like a lotus, was pleased: / 'I am pleased with this wise man,' [said] the Lord to Nārada.
Then once, Nārada, who knows the supreme truth, / of exceedingly great splendour, like the sun in bodily form, went to that region.
Desiring to see that treasure of austerities, Puṇḍarīka, the divine one, / his soul filled with devotion to Viṣṇu, engaged in the welfare of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Seeing Nārada arrive, adorned with an aura of splendour, / of great intellect, exceedingly generous, the sole receptacle of all the Vedas,
with joined palms and bowing low, with an overjoyed inner soul, / having offered the guest-offering according to rule, he bowed once again.
'Who is this of exceedingly wonderful appearance, resplendent, wearing pleasing dress, / holding a musical instrument in his hand, fair-faced, adorned with a victory garland,
Vivasvat, or Agni, or Indra, or Varuṇa?' / Thus reflecting as he stood, he spoke to the one of supreme splendour:
Puṇḍarīka said: / 'Who are you who have arrived here, or whence [do you come], O one of supreme splendour? / For sight of you, O venerable lord, is generally difficult to attain on earth.
No man equal to you has ever been seen by me, O lord; / you ought to tell me completely what has been asked by me, O sinless one.'
Nārada said: / 'I am Nārada, arrived out of curiosity to see you, / an enduringly devoted servant of the Lord, a devotee like you, O twice-born one.
Remembered, gladdened, or worshipped, a devotee of the Lord, / even if born a caṇḍāla, cleanses by chance [contact], O best of the twice-born.
I am a servant of Vāsudeva, the God of gods, bearer of the Śārṅga bow, / who holds the conch, disc, and mace in his hands, the sole eye of the three worlds.'
Thus addressed by Nārada whose mind was overwhelmed with devotion, / greatly astonished by the sight of him, he spoke sweetly to the Brahmin:
Puṇḍarīka said: / 'Blessed am I among embodied beings; worthy of worship even by the gods am I! / My ancestors are fulfilled today; the fruit of my birth has been attained!
Grant your grace, O divine sage, especially to one devoted to you! / I, whirled about by my own past actions, will perform whatever [you instruct], O wise one.'
You should teach the supreme, secret duty to be done; / you are the refuge of all living beings, especially of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Nārada said: / Many are the scriptures here, and likewise the rituals, O twice-born; / manifold is the category of dharma, and similarly the mind on earth.
And distinctiveness of the world arises precisely from that, O best of the twice-born; / otherwise, how could there be happiness or suffering for all living beings?
This world is mere consciousness, momentary, devoid of self— / thus has it been understood by some, independent of external objects.
This world is continuously born from the unmanifest, the eternal from the eternal— / so others say; and into that very source it dissolves.
The selves are declared to be many, eternal, and all-pervading / by others, the foremost of thinkers, intent on observing the reality.
Still others hold the self to be coextensive with the body, / even in the body of an elephant, an insect, etc., and in the great cosmic egg.
Just as the functioning of the world is today, so also in other times; / this flow is altogether eternal; who is the maker? — so say some.
Whatever is not an object of direct perception does not exist here; / whence are heaven and the like? — so say others with disciplined minds.
Some say this [world] is without a Lord; others say it has a Lord; / having exceedingly divided opinions, turning their backs on the ultimate truth.
Thus even other deceptive theorists, according to their intellect and according to what they have heard, / speak with various differences, establishing their own reasoning.
Becoming attentive regarding dialectical arguments, I declare, O rich in asceticism, / this auspicious ultimate truth, destroyer of terrible saṃsāra.
The gods and other men acknowledge its root; / they are grasped by valid means of knowledge; not so by those deluded about valid knowledge.
That which is future, past, and exceedingly distant, / is not apprehended according to capacity, being fixed on present objects.

Sacred tradition has been proclaimed by the sages, handed down in succession from an ancient form; / that should indeed be understood as the valid means of knowledge that establishes the ultimate truth.
The knowledge which, through the power of repeated practice, destroys the stain of passion and hatred, / that is produced, O best of the twice-born; that is known by the name of sacred tradition.
The fruit and the action, reality, discernment, view, and the all-pervading [Lord], / free from conceptual construction of genus and the like—this is the second mark of sacred tradition.
Consciousness of the Self is eternal, beginningless, beyond the senses, / pure consciousness, immortal, to be known, infinite, unborn, imperishable.
Existing within the manifest through the nature of both manifest and unmanifest, undefiled; / known as Viṣṇu because of pervading, standing distinct from what is known.
To be meditated upon by yogins, unknowable by those averse to the ultimate truth; / it is perceived by intellects as distinct, yet it is not divided in the Self.
Listen attentively, dear child; I will declare to you, O sinless one, / what was formerly spoken by Brahmā when I asked him, O you of good vows.
Once, bowing down properly to Brahmā the Grandfather, dwelling in the world of Brahmā, / I questioned the unborn and imperishable one:
What is declared to be supreme knowledge, and what is considered supreme yoga? / Explain this to me in truth, O Brahmā, O Grandfather!
Brahmā said: / Listen attentively, dear child, to the unsurpassed yoga of knowledge, / concise in text, rich in meaning, whose practice of worship is free from sorrow.
The Puruṣa who is spoken of in tradition as the twenty-fifth; / he alone is the soul of all beings, and by that he is designated.
Nārāyaṇa is the abode of the universe, the eternal Supreme Self, / dedicated to the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the universe.
And he is the one eternal God of gods among the three selves; / he is always to be worshiped, O brāhmaṇa; they behold the Lord of the Universe.
As the state of the universe is now, so again at other times; / past, present, and future, and likewise what is remote,
gross, subtle, and otherwise—they see with the eye of knowledge, / their minds fixed on Him, their life breaths dedicated to Him, devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Otherwise it appears to the dull-witted, wicked souls, / corrupted by the knowledge of false reasoning, advocates of isolated senses.
Nārada said: / Let another matter also be heard as spoken by me, O sinless one, / as it was proclaimed formerly by Brahmā, the causal soul of the universe.
To the gods headed by Indra, and to the sages, O you of good vows, / the lotus-seated one declared beneficial words as they inquired.
Brahmā said: / Dharma is focused on Nārāyaṇa, and the eternal worlds are focused on Nārāyaṇa; / sacrifices are focused on Nārāyaṇa, and diverse scriptures are focused on Nārāyaṇa.
The Vedas with their auxiliary limbs and other texts too are Viṣṇu, Hari, the lord of the universe; / the five elements, earth and the rest, are he, the imperishable one, O gods.
The entire world should be known by the gods as consisting of Viṣṇu; / nevertheless, deluded humans, O wicked one, do not know this.
This moving and unmoving world is pervaded by his illusion alone; / he whose mind is fixed on him, whose vital breath has gone to him, knows, being a knower of the highest truth.
Viṣṇu is the lord of all beings, the protector of the three worlds; / in him this entire universe abides and also comes into being.
Rudra dissolves the universe; Viṣṇu is declared for protection; / and I myself am here for its creation, and likewise the other world guardians.
The support of all, without support, complete and without parts, / subtle, vast, and yet beyond that, higher than the high.
Go to him alone for refuge, who carries out the destruction of everything; / he is our father and progenitor, celebrated as Madhusūdana.
Having been addressed thus by lotus-born Brahmā, all the gods / bowed to the lord of all worlds, the god Viṣṇu, Janārdana.
Therefore you too, O sage among brahmins, become devoted to Nārāyaṇa; / who else other than he is so exceedingly generous that he can grant what is asked?
Accept that Puruṣottama alone as your father and mother, / the lord of the world, god of gods, master of the universe.
By this fire offering, by austerity, and by study, / one should constantly and unweariedly please the master, the god over the lords of gods.
Pleasure in heaven is transient, and it is something merely to be performed; / accept him alone, Puruṣottama, O sage among brahmins.
What use are many mantras to him? What use are many vows to him? / The mantra "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" accomplishes all aims.
Whether clad in bark or matted-haired, O brahmin, carrying a staff or shaven-headed, / or adorned, O best of brahmins, outward sign is not the cause of dharma.
Even those cruel and wicked souls who are always devoted to sinful conduct / go to the supreme abode if they are dedicated to Nārāyaṇa.
Free from sin, they are not tainted by streams of evils, [becoming] Vaiṣṇavas;
with minds subdued through non-violence, they purify the entire world.
The king celebrated as Kṣatrabandhu, who slaughtered living creatures, / attained the supreme Vaiṣṇava abode from Keśava's dwelling.
Ambarīṣa, a king of great virtue, knower of the highest truth, / having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa, attained the Vaiṣṇava state.
Many other tranquil brahmin seers of strict vows, / having meditated on the supreme self, attained supreme perfection.
Prahlāda, of supreme joy, formerly served, / worshipped, and meditated upon Nārāyaṇa Hari, and was protected by him alone.
The glorious king named Bharata, supremely righteous, / having worshipped him for a long time, attained supreme liberation.
Whether a student, a householder, a forest hermit, or an ascetic, / abandoned of Keśava's worship, they do not attain the supreme path.
He in whom such an understanding arises over thousands of births, / [thinking,] "I am a servant of the devotees of Viṣṇu," accomplishes all aims.
That person reaches the world of Viṣṇu, there is no doubt in this; / what more then of men whose vital breath has gone to him and who observe strict vows?
He should constantly be meditated upon with undivided mind by seekers of truth: / Nārāyaṇa, who pervades the universe, the eternal supreme self.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, the celestial seer vanished right there, / Nārada, devoted to the welfare of others, knower of the supreme truth.
The righteous Puṇḍarīka too, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, / chanting the eight-syllable mantra, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa,"
always uttering the words, "Be gracious to me, O soul of the universe!" / established Govinda, whose nature is nectar, in the lotus of his heart.
Rich in austerities, the ascetic lived for a long time alone / in pure, serene Śālagrāma, free from duality and without possessions.
Even in a dream that great-minded one saw nothing other than Keśava; / even sleep was never an obstacle to the aims of life for him.
Through austerity, celibacy, and purity in particular, / and according as impressions arose through life after life,
by the grace of the god of gods, the witness of all the world, / he, free from sin, attained supreme Vaiṣṇava perfection.
He saw Acyuta, holding a conch, discus, and mace in hand, clad in yellow garments, / dark, lotus-eyed, of eternal form.
Lions, tigers, and other beasts that kill living creatures, / abandoned their natural enmity and gathered in his presence.
They roamed as they pleased with their sensory dispositions delighted, / having achieved delightful mutual welfare, O son of Pāṇḍu.
Likewise, the water of the lakes and rivers became clear, / and the seasons were pleasant, endowed with pure senses.
The winds were pleasant to touch, and the trees were laden with flowers and fruits; / all things turned favourable to that wise one.
Everything became gracious to him; the moving and unmoving was pleased, / when Govinda, the god of gods, fond of devotees, was pleased.
Then one day, the blessed one, the lord of the universe, / having large lotus-like eyes, appeared to the wise Puṇḍarīka.
Holding a conch, discus, and mace in hand, clad in yellow garments, resplendent, / with wide lotus eyes and a face resembling the disc of the moon,
wearing small bells, earrings, necklaces, armlets, and a waistband, / marked with the Śrīvatsa, clad in yellow garments, adorned with the Kaustubha jewel,
his body encircled by a forest garland, with gleaming diadem and earrings, / and with a radiant sacred thread draped with strings of pearls,
the lord of gods shone with fly-whisks, fans, and other emblems, / being served by gods, Siddhas together with Indra, Gandharvas, excellent munis,
Yakṣas, excellent Nāgas, and celestial nymphs. / Having seen that god of gods, the sinless Puṇḍarīka himself,
then with his intellect praised the great-souled Janārdana, / having bowed with hands joined in reverence, his inner soul filled with joy.
Puṇḍarīka said: Obeisance be to you, Viṣṇu, the sole eye of all the world, / taintless, eternal, beyond qualities, the supreme self.
You are the lord of all beings, and likewise without any lord above you; / likewise Govinda, bearing the Garuḍa banner, for destroying fear and distress.
Out of grace to beings you assume multiple forms; / they say that all this is in you, and solely composed of you.
You are distinct from this universe, and the universe is made by you; / obeisance, repeated obeisance to the lotus born from your navel.
Obeisance to you whose self-manifest power is renowned in all the Upaniṣads; / you alone are the cause of all gods, O crusher of Kaiṭabha.
Be pleased, O dweller in the heart, bearer of conch, discus, and mace! / Obeisance to the supporter of the earth, the first origin of all beings,
to Viṣṇu of multiform shapes, the almighty one, / whose greatness Brahmā and the other chief gods do not comprehend,
which is measurable only by austerity; to you I bow. / Beyond the reach of words, your greatness is not attained.
Untouched by caste and the like, you are ever to be meditated on in truth, / and likewise in differentiated forms through compassion for devotees,
you are seen in the form of a fish, a tortoise, and others, O Puruṣottama. / Bhīṣma said: Puṇḍarīka, praising the lord of the world, Puruṣottama,
The heroic [Prajāpati] looked upon him alone, whose sight had long been prayed for. / The Blessed Viṣṇu, lotus-navelled, who took the three strides, addressed him—
addressed the illustrious Puṇḍarīka with a voice deep as thunder:
The Blessed One said: / I am pleased, my child; blessing upon you, O noble-minded Puṇḍarīka! / Choose a boon; I will give whatever is in your heart.
Hearing these spoken words of the God of gods, / the noble-minded Puṇḍarīka petitioned thus:
Puṇḍarīka said: / Where am I, extremely dull-witted, and where are you, who desire my welfare? / Whatever is beneficial for me, O Lord of gods, command that, O Mādhava!
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, very pleased, then spoke / to the illustrious Puṇḍarīka, who stood before him with folded hands:
Come, may it be well with you; along with me, O man of firm vows! / You are beneficial and your nature is eternal; remain always with me.
Bhīṣma said: / When the Bearer of Śrī, affectionate to devotees, had spoken thus with love, / kettledrums sounded in heaven and a rain of flowers fell.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā, cried: “Well done! Well done!” / Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras sang especially.
Taking him right there, the God of gods, Lord of the universe, / mounted upon Garuḍa, departed, revered by all the worlds.
Therefore you too, O king of kings, endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, / with your mind on him, your breath devoted to him, engaged in the welfare of his devotees,
worship the Supreme Person appropriately and adore him; / listen to his holy story that destroys all evil.
By whichever means, O king of kings, one endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu / pleases the Universal Soul, do that in extensive detail.
Even having sacrificed with hundreds of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, / men whose faces are turned away from Nārāyaṇa do not attain [him].
By whoever the two syllables “Hari” are uttered even once, / he has girded his loins for going to liberation.
Theirs is the gain, theirs is the victory; whence could defeat come to them / in whose heart Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus, dwells?
Whoever constantly hears this or reads it with concentrated mind, / freed from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Īśvara said: / Having heard this glorification of the Name, O daughter of the mountain, / righteousness, wealth, pleasure, and liberation certainly come to be; there is no doubt.
The Brahmin born in a pure family who is devoted to the Veda, / a Vaiṣṇava, is an embodiment of Viṣṇu; no other twice-born is so at any time.
Uttering the name of Viṣṇu with his mouth, intent on meditation in his heart, / bearing the conch and discus, wise, wearing a garland made of tulasī,
he is to be known as liberated while alive; having enjoyed pleasures repeatedly, / he rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu along with twenty-one generations of his family.
Puṇḍarīka was liberated according to his capacity; there is no doubt in this. / Through devotional disposition Govinda attains everlasting satisfaction.
In Kali, singing of Hari in one’s own home, especially, / is declared equal to chanting the Sāmas in concentrations of worship to the gods.

6.81.m: Pārvatī said: / Speak again, O noble-minded one, of the glorification of the Gaṅgā, / hearing which all the sages repeatedly become free from passion.
Of what kind is her glorification, O Lord of all, O master? / Her origin was heard previously, but her greatness was not heard by me. / You are the origin of all beings, and you are the eternal god.
Mahādeva said: / Sages came to see Bhīṣma lying on the bed of arrows, / who was equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect and equal to Śakra in valour:
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, / Aṅgiras, Gautama, Agastya, and formerly the self-restrained Sumati,
Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, the omniscient lord of the Pramathas, / Raibhya, Bṛhaspati, Vyāsa, the purifier Kaśyapa, Dhruva,
Durvāsas, Jamadagni, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Gālava, / Uśanas, then Bharadvāja, Kratu, and Āstīka,
Sthūlākṣa, Sarvalokākṣa, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Kuśa, / Nārada, Parvata, Sudhanvan, and the twice-born Cyavana,
Matibhū, Bhuvana, Dhaumya, Śatānanda, Kṛtavraṇa, / and Rāma son of Jamadagni, Ṛcīka, and the others.
Bowing to them duly, the son of Dharma along with his younger brothers / worshipped those majestic sages, worthy of the world's worship, according to rule.
Those great-souled ascetics, worshipped and seated comfortably, / engaged in conversations concerning Bhīṣma and concerning heavenly virtues.
At that discourse of those sages whose minds were purified, / Yudhiṣṭhira, bowing his head to Bhīṣma, asked this:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Which regions are greatly holy, which mountains, and which hermitages, / that should always be frequented by those seeking righteousness? Tell me that, O grandfather!
Bhīṣma said: / Right in this connection, O best of men, they cite this legendary history: / the conversation between a gleaner and an accomplished adept, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
A certain accomplished adept, having wandered over this entire earth, / reached the house of the great-souled Śibi, who lived by gleaning ears of corn, O king.
He knew the true nature of the knowledge of the Self, his senses were always subdued, / free from attachment and aversion, skilled in knowledge and deeds,
always foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to the duties of Viṣṇu, / not reviling Vaiṣṇavas, ever devoted to righteousness,
ever devoted to the practice of yoga, bearing the conch and discus, / knowing the truth of worship at the three junctures of the day, ever devoted to Śrīkaṇṭha,
learned in the knowledge of the Vedas, discerning righteousness and unrighteousness, / always vowed to recite the Veda, and constantly honouring guests.
Endowed with reverence for sacred bathing-places, he always lived by gleaning; / whatever meditation in the four Vedas was sung by the Self-born,
the twice-born bearing the very form of Viṣṇu knew all that; / clear in various principles of righteousness, his mind was always set on the imperishable.
At one time he went to the house of Śibi; / and seeing him, the noble-minded [Śibi], having offered hospitality according to rule,
Śibi inquired about the cause of welfare among regions.
The gleaner said: / Which regions, which inhabited lands, which mountains, and which hermitages / are holy, O best of the twice-born? Please point them out to me out of affection.
The accomplished adept said: / Those regions, those inhabited lands, those mountains, and those hermitages / are holy, in the midst of which is ever the Tripathagā, the best of rivers.
By asceticism, by celibacy, by sacrifices, or again by renunciation, / a creature does not obtain that destination which one obtains by resorting to the Gaṅgā.
The satisfaction that comes to self-controlled men / who have bathed in its waters, related to Gaṅgā, is not [attained] even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Just as the sun, rising, shines having dispelled thick darkness, / so one bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā shines having dispelled sin.
Just as a heap of cotton perishes upon meeting fire, O twice-born, / so plunging into the Gaṅgā removes all evil.
He who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā heated by the sun’s rays, / freed from the mist of ignorance, is indeed superior to fire.
A man who performs a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa penances on one foot, / and a man who bathes in the Gaṅgā—the latter is indeed superior.
A man who hangs upside down for ten thousand years, / and the best of men who serves the water of the Gaṅgā for a single month:
the latter is freed from the murder of a brahmin and goes to Viṣṇu's sorrowless realm. / This Veṇī is equally sacred, purifying, and destructive of sin,
by the mere remembrance of which the killer of a child is instantly freed. / That Prayāga is the king of tirthas, hard to attain indeed for Vaiṣṇavas.
Bathing where, O best of men, one quickly goes to Vaikuṇṭha. / He knows not pleasant nor unpleasant; he encounters neither virtue nor vice.
And by merely bathing in the Gaṅgā, one is freed from great sin.
Whoever says ‘Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,’ even from hundreds of leagues away, / is freed from all sins and goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Whether the killer of a brahmin, or a cow-killer, a drinker of liquor, or a child-slayer, / he is freed from all sins and quickly goes to heaven.
By beholding Mādhava, and likewise beholding the best [lord], / and taking a bath at the Veṇī, one proceeds to Vaikuṇṭha.
Just as darkness vanishes when the sun has risen, / even so sins are destroyed by merely bathing in it.
At Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, the Nīla mountain, / and having bathed at the Kanakhala tirtha, rebirth does not occur.
Knowing thus, O best of men, one who repeatedly bathes in the Gaṅgā, / by the mere bathing, O king, is freed from all guilt.
Among the gods the foremost is Viṣṇu; among sacrifices, the horse sacrifice; / the Aśvattha among all trees; and always the river Bhāgīrathī [among rivers].

6.82.m: Pārvatī said: / What kind of characteristic of Vaiṣṇavas has been expounded, / and what kind of greatness? Speak, O Lord Viśveśvara!
Mahādeva said: / Since he is proclaimed as Viṣṇu's, he is considered a Vaiṣṇava. / He is to be known as the origin of all, and then assuming the form of Brahmā,
from whom were born the brahmins who have mastered the Vedas. / They are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas, and never any others.
Endowed with purity, truth, and forbearance, free from passion and aversion, / knowing the inquiry into Vedic learning—he is called a Vaiṣṇava.
Constantly devoted to the Agnihotra fire-rite, always honoring guests, / devoted to his father, devoted to his mother—he alone is called a Vaiṣṇava.
Endowed with compassion and virtue, and averted from sin, / marked with the conch and the discus—he alone is called a Vaiṣṇava.
He who wears a garland around his neck, always utters 'Rāma' with his mouth, / and constantly sings [of him] with devotion—that man is known as a Vaiṣṇava.
Always devoted to the Purāṇas, constantly engaged in sacrifices, / those men are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas, approved in all duties.
Those men who commit sins and revile them / die and repeatedly enter wretched wombs.
And the twice-born who constantly worship the image named Gopāla, / fashioned purely of metal, well adorned, with four hands—
those brahmins who perform such worship are known as sharers of merit. / Having made an image carved of stone named Kṛṣṇa, of beautiful form,
the brahmins who perform worship are known as embodiments of merit. / Where there is a Śālagrāma stone and where there is a Dvāravatī stone,
where there is the conjunction of both, there is liberation, without a doubt. / If one installs the image with mantra and performs worship,

that worship bears ten-millionfold merit, granting virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation. / Ninefold devotion should indeed be performed there towards Janārdana. / Therefore, an image made of stone as well as one made of metal [should be made] by you.
In it, meditation and worship should be performed by devotees; / there, in that image, one should provide worship fit for royalty.
One should always remember the Lord Adhokṣaja, the Soul of all, / the sole refuge of the poor and helpless, the cause of the livelihood of the worlds.
In that image one should continually remember the destroyer of great sins, / saying: 'This is Gopāla, this is Kṛṣṇa, this is Rāma.'
He who properly performs worship is indeed a Bhāgavata man. / Just as the form assumed by Keśava in Gokula,
such a form should be fashioned by Vaiṣṇavas, the best of men. / For the satisfaction of one's soul, the wise person should have that very form fashioned,
from which abundant devotion arises, without a doubt. / The conch, the discus, the mace, and the other weapons of Viṣṇu
should be fashioned in that image especially according to prescribed proportions: / four-armed, two-eyed, holding the conch, discus, and mace,
clad in yellow garments, radiant and venerable, / wearing a forest garland, with shining beryl earrings,
with a jewel attached to the crown, ever illumined by the Kaustubha. / Made of gold, or silver, or copper, or brass,
it should be caused to be made with supreme devotion by Vaiṣṇavas, the best of the twice-born, / and having installed it especially with Vedic mantras prescribed in the Āgamas,
the worship should then be performed in accordance with the scriptures, / performing worship with the sixteen services and mantras according to rule.
When the Lord of the Universe is worshipped, all the gods are worshipped; / therefore, by this method the Great Lord should be worshipped.
The god without beginning or end, holding the conch, discus, and mace, / the Lord of All gives everything to the meritorious Vaiṣṇavas.
As is Viṣṇu, so is Śarva; no difference exists anywhere. / Knowing this, O goddess, the fashioning of the image of both [is approved].

One who performs worship of Śiva while being intent on reviling Viṣṇu / dwells in the Raurava hells, without a doubt.

I am Viṣṇu, I am Rudra, and I am Brahmā the grandfather; / I constantly dwell in all beings again and again.
Pārvatī said: / Who are the servants? Who are the Vaiṣṇavas? And who are celebrated as devotees on earth? / Tell me their characteristics according to truth, O Maheśvara.
Mahādeva said: / Even Śūdras become servants and Vaiṣṇavas—Nārada and the rest; / Prahlāda and Ambarīṣa and others are his devotees, O delighter of the Gaṇas.
He who is constantly devoted to rites honoring Brahman, who recites the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, / and who is marked with the conch and discus—he alone is called a Vaiṣṇava.
Always devoted to serving the twice-born, always worshipping Viṣṇu, / he listens extensively to the Purāṇa which is on par with the Veda.
That śūdra is called a servant of Hari, O delighter of the mountain. / Resorting to devotion from the age of five in diverse ways,
he is declared to be a devotee, esteemed among all virtuous people. / They are to be known as Dhruva and others, and those like Ambarīṣa and others,
and they are declared by the sages to be devotees at all times, O radiant lady. / In the Kali age, the most blessed are śūdras wholly dedicated to meditation on Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, they go to the eternal realm of Viṣṇu. / He who is marked with the conch and discus, who practices devotion to Viṣṇu,
and who especially performs the fourfold great festival, / that śūdra is a servant of Viṣṇu, as seen and heard.

6.85.m: On the eleventh day, O best among the gods, preceded by the preliminary consecration, / worship should be performed there at night with devotion by the Vaiṣṇavas.
God of gods, homage to you; Śrī Viśveśa, homage to you! / Lord of Rati, homage to you; homage to you, ornament of the universe!
O Mahādeva, homage to you, homage to you, creator of the universe! / Accept the offering of water, O Lord, and grant me liberation at all times!”
One should worship the one seated on Garuḍa with various kinds of fine flowers; / freed from all obstacles, he attains union with Viṣṇu.
Keeping a night-vigil there on the twelfth lunar day, well-concentrated, / he should adore the god, immutable and imperishable Viṣṇu, preceded by devotion.
Thus, this festival connected with Vaiśākha, named after Viṣṇu, / should be performed with a devotional disposition by those dedicated to it, who desire devotion.
One should cause the rite to be performed there with the mantra declared in the āgamas; / when it is performed, O Mahādevī, the fruit is equal to ten million sacrifices.
Free from passion and aversion, setting aside great delusion, / having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the eternal [abode] of Viṣṇu.
A brāhmaṇa who performs the festival on earth with a devotional disposition, / freed from all sins, certainly goes to Vaikuṇṭha.
Even if destitute of Vedic study, and devoid of the study of the sacred treatises, / upon attaining devotion to Hari, he attains the realm of Viṣṇu.

Delighting in the self, always liberated, he becomes one who has conquered himself; / and he indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu as long as the moon and sun endure.

Eighty-sixth chapter. Mahādeva said: / When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, there is the rite of investing the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa), / by performing which, O goddess of gods, divine devotion arises.

The investment of Viṣṇu's sacred thread should be performed with faith by the wise; / O Pārvatī, his annual worship [thereby] becomes complete.

Through the investment of Viṣṇu's sacred thread, happiness of oneself arises; / when Viṣṇu is constantly worshipped, one attains manifold joy.

Having brought thread or cloth spun by a Brahmin woman, / or with thread spun by oneself, one should have it made.

Or thread spun by a virtuous Śūdra woman may likewise be accepted; / otherwise, even by purchase, it should be obtained in due manner.

The rite of placing the sacred thread should be performed with linen; / or the sacred thread, sacred to Viṣṇu, should be made of silver.

or, O goddess of gods, it should be made of gold according to rule. / In the absence of all metals, thread should be taken by the wise.

Having made the thread threefold and washed it with water, / its measure for a liṅga is according to the liṅga, and according to rule for an image.

the thirteenth belongs to Kāma, and the fourteenth is declared for Śarva; / similarly, the fifteenth is known for the worship of the Creator (Dhātṛ).

These lunar days are declared suitable for investing the sacred thread. / Twelve [knots] are declared for the inferior, twice that is taught for the intermediate,

and thrice that for the superior are the knots on the sacred thread. / Having dyed all of it with camphor and saffron, or with sandalwood and turmeric,

it should be placed in a new basket. / Where the worship of the deity takes place, they should be placed like deities.

Having first worshipped the deity, and perfumed the sacred thread, / when the sacred thread has been consecrated, worship is then taught.

One should draw near to those gods who reside in the sacred threads: / Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the three deities of the strands.

Kriyā, Pauruṣī, Vīrā, and fourthly Aparājitā, / Jayā, Vijayā, Muktidā, Sadāśivā,

Manonmanī as the ninth, and tenthly Sarvatomukhī: / one should install the deities of the knots into the threads.

Then, having invoked them with the invocation gesture (āvāhanamudrā) according to the rule declared in the scriptures, / bringing them together in proximity (saṃnidhīkaraṇa) there completely is prescribed:

having performed sprinkling with the mantra taught in the Āgama, having sprinkled with the mantra 'klīṃ kṛṣṇāya', and offering perfume, incense, a lamp,

food offerings, and the like, offering betel and the like, having worshipped the deities of the sacred thread with the sixteen services of worship and so forth,

’Invited, O Great God, together with the Goddess, the Gaṇas, and others, / or with mantras, the world-protectors, and attendants,

come, O Lord Viṣṇu, for the sake of completing the ritual! / In the morning we will perform your worship; make your presence constant!’

having performed one's duties, amidst the auspicious reciting of prayers for a blessed day, shouts of 'Victory! Victory!', and the sounds of bells and other musical instruments,

Then one should perform great worship of Viṣṇu that pleases him, / by the performance of which, O goddess, Viṣṇu, the Self, is pleased.
A row of lamps all around should be arranged according to rule, / and the wise man should prepare four kinds of food offerings.
Then one should offer the sacred threads that have been worshipped, O beautiful one; / and with devotion, especially, one should then worship the venerable guru.

The great guru is to be worshipped with garments and ornaments according to rule; / having worshipped the guru there, one should then put on the sacred thread.

Then, to whichever Vaiṣṇavas are present, having offered them betel and the like, offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire, to Śrīnivāsa, to glorious
’Lacking mantra, lacking ritual action, and lacking devotion, O Keśava, / whatever worship has been performed by me, may it certainly become complete!’

Then, having dismissed [the deities], one should oneself eat sweet food together with beloved kin and with Vaiṣṇava Brahmins. / Best of Brahmins who hear this divine worship, / freed from all sins, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
As long as the moon shines, as long as the sun shines, / so long does the investor of the sacred thread shine [in heaven]; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever gifts and observances there are on earth, / all of them indeed attain completeness when the investment of the sacred thread is performed.
And this rite of placing the sacred thread is the king of festivals; / a slayer of a Brahmin is purified therein—no doubt should be entertained here.
"True, true, again I say true, O daughter of the mountain: / as great merit is declared in investing the sacred thread, so too merely in witnessing it.
Or, O fortunate lady, by whichever Śūdras the rite of placing the sacred thread / has been performed with a devotional disposition, they are indeed considered most blessed.
Fortunate am I, my purpose accomplished am I, blessed on the surface of the earth, / for I have offered that Vaiṣṇava devotion which bestows liberation."

6.85.m:
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, entitled 'The Placing of the Sacred Thread,' in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

Eighty-seventh chapter. Maheśvara said: / "In Caitra, with campaka flowers or with jātī blossoms, / Keśava, the destroyer of distress, should be zealously worshipped.

With damanaka and maruka leaves, or even with bilva blossoms, / one should worship the Lord of the worlds, Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords.

Likewise with divine lotuses or red flowers, with concentrated mind, / men should worship Viṣṇu in the month of Caitra, O ruler of the gods.

In Vaiśākha, O goddess, the great Lord should always be worshipped / taking ketakī petals when the sun is stationed in Taurus.

By whomsoever Hari is worshipped with devotion, he is pleased for a hundred manvantaras. / When the month of Jyeṣṭha arrives, one should worship him with various flowers.

When the God of gods is worshipped, all the gods are well worshipped. / Even having committed thousands of sins and hundreds of great sins,

they too will go, O goddess, where Viṣṇu is together with Śrī. / When the month of Āṣāḍha arrives, one should perform worship in a special manner.

6.85.m:
With oleander, with red flowers, or always with lotuses, / men who perform the worship of Viṣṇu are to be known as sharers of merit.

Those who will worship Viṣṇu, Govinda, with kadamba flowers / that resemble gold, have no fear born of Yama.

At the arrival of the rains, he who is dark as a raincloud, worshipped with kadamba blossoms, / grants cherished desires for as long as fourteen Indras reign.

Just as Mādhava rejoices upon obtaining Lakṣmī, / so does the Creator of the world rejoice upon receiving a kadamba flower.

With tulasī, black tulasī, or with vañjula blossoms, O ruler of the gods, / Viṣṇu, constantly worshipped, perpetually removes suffering.

When the month of Śrāvaṇa arrives, those who worship Janārdana, / taking flax blossoms and dūrvā grass blades,

he is to be worshipped with effort, especially with various flowers; / he grants abundant desires until the dissolution of all beings.

When the month of Bhādrapada arrives, listen, O daughter of the mountain: / with campakas or white flowers, or with red sindūraka blossoms,

Or with white water-lilies, O great goddess, one obtains the fruit of all desires; / Viṣṇu's worship should indeed be performed in the auspicious month of Āśvina.

6.85.m:
With yūthikās, fresh jātīs, and various auspicious flowers, / he should always be zealously worshipped by people with devotion.

Those men on earth who worship Janārdana by bringing lotuses / attain dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

When the month of Kārtika arrives, the Great Lord is to be worshipped. / As many seasonal flowers as there are, they are to be offered to Mādhava.

With sesame seeds or sesame flowers one should perform worship. / When the Lord of gods is worshipped, one enjoys boundless fruit.

Those who will worship Janārdana in Kārtika with bakula blossoms, / punnāgas, or campakas—they are gods, not mortals.

In Mārgaśīrṣa the Lord should always be zealously worshipped / with various flowers, food offerings, incenses, and wave-offerings of light.

In Mārgaśīrṣa one should especially worship with divine flowers. / In the month of Pauṣa, O great goddess, good worship is declared to grant auspiciousness:

with various tulasī leaves and with musk water. / When the month of Māgha arrives, one should worship him with various flowers.

When the God of gods is worshipped, one surely obtains what is desired. / Likewise, worship with camphor and various food offerings and sweetmeats [is recommended].

And when Phālguna arrives, the worship of Mādhava / should be performed as a spring ritual, bringing flowers of every kind.

With fresh flowers, O ruler of gods, or with all available flowers one should then worship. / And when the Lord of the universe is worshipped, a person constantly attains / the imperishable abode of Vaikuṇṭha through the grace of holy Viṣṇu."

Eighty-eighth chapter. Sūta said: Hereafter the glorification of Kārtika is set forth. / Sūta said: Once, a sage came to Dvārakā desiring to see Kṛṣṇa, / bringing divine flowers that grew from the wish-granting tree.

Kṛṣṇa extended hospitality to Nārada with a welcome; / saying, "Here is the arghya, here is the water for washing feet," he offered him a seat.

Nārada presented those flowers to Kṛṣṇa; / and Kṛṣṇa distributed them among his sixteen thousand wives.

Forgetting Satyabhāmā, the Lord gave them to all the others. / Thereupon, enraged, Satyabhāmā entered the chamber of anger.

Knowing this, Kṛṣṇa went there composed in mind; / consoling Satyabhāmā, he called Garuḍa to mind.

As soon as he was remembered, Garuḍa came and stood before him. / Mounting that winged bird in haste, the Lord spoke to his beloved:

6.85.m:
"O Satya, do not be angry; for your sake, having fought with the gods / and opposed the king of the gods, I shall plant in your courtyard

the wish-granting tree, O highly fortunate lady; forgive my offense." / Having made this promise, Kṛṣṇa, together with Satyabhāmā,

went swiftly to the world of the gods, where the slayer of Vṛtra dwelt. / Asked for the wish-granting tree, [Indra] answered the Lord:

"This divine tree is not suitable to be obtained on earth by you, O Lord." / Then the mighty-armed, powerful one grew furious, uprooted the tree by its roots,

and quickly loaded it onto his mount. / Thereupon the wielder of the thunderbolt, powerful, swiftly raised his thunderbolt

and struck Garuḍa, saying, "Release the wish-granting tree!" / Then the bird, out of respect even for the thunderbolt,

dropped a single feather and quickly flew away. / From that blow of the thunderbolt three birds came to be:

the peacock, the mongoose, and the blue jay. Kṛṣṇa then went to Dvārāvatī. / Having arrived, he planted it in Satyabhāmā's home. / Just then Nārada arrived, greatly honored by Satya.

Satyabhāmā said: / "How is such a wish-granting tree, and such a husband and lord, / to be obtained in life after life? Please tell me that!"

6.85.m:
Thus questioned, Nārada, the best of sages, then said: / 'This is attained, O Satyabhāmā, through the gift of a man's weight in gold.'

Then Satyabhāmā gave Kṛṣṇa together with the wish-granting tree / to Nārada, after weighing him according to rule. / Taking all the equipment, Nārada went to heaven.

Sūta said: When the best of divine sages had departed after bidding farewell to the Lord of Śrī, / Satyā, her face blossoming with joy, then spoke to Vāsudeva.

Satyabhāmā said: / "I am blessed, my purpose is accomplished, and my life has borne fruit; / and blessed are my parents, the cause of my birth,

who surely brought me forth as the most fortunate woman in the three worlds, / since I am the beloved wife among your sixteen thousand wives!"

Because I properly offered the Primordial Person / together with the wish-fulfilling tree to Nārada according to the prescribed rule,

and although even the report of it is known to creatures dwelling on earth, / that very wish-granting tree now stands in my home.

And I am exceedingly dear to the Lord of Śrī, the sovereign of the three worlds. / Therefore, O Madhusūdana, I wish to ask you something.

If you wish to do what pleases me, tell it here in detail; / and having heard it, I shall again do what is good for myself,

Sūta said:
Hearing these words of his beloved, the elder brother of Gada smiled, his face beaming.

Taking Satyabhāmā's hand in his, he went to the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree, / having playfully waved away his attendants, accompanied by his beloved.

Smiling and addressing Satyā, the Lord of the worlds, / his bodily hairs bristling with joy to please and gratify her, spoke:

Kṛṣṇa said:
"There is no other fair-hipped woman dearer to me than you. / Among the sixteen thousand women, O beloved, you are equal to my very life.

For your sake arose enmity with the king of gods and the deities. / Whatever you request, O lovely one, even if it be difficult to hear, it shall be done.

Even that which should not be given, or cannot be done, or cannot even be spoken— / how could I not answer a question asked by you, O beloved? / Ask whatever is in your mind; I will tell you everything."

Satyabhāmā said:
"What gift, vow, or asceticism did I perform before, / by which, though born a mortal among mortals, I have indeed become like Bhavānī?

Ever sharing half of your body, riding upon Garuḍa, / I have gone with you to the abode of Indra and the deities.

Therefore I wish to ask you: what good deed did I do? / And in another birth, what was my conduct, who was I, and whose daughter was I?"

6.85.m:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen with a focused mind, O beloved, to the meritorious vow / that you performed in your previous birth; I will tell you all of it.

At the end of the Kṛta age, there was in Māyāpurī an excellent twice-born, / an Ātreya named Devaśarman, who had mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.

Hospitable to guests, devoted to serving the sacred fire, dedicated to vows for the Sun, / constantly worshiping the Sun, he was like another Sun incarnate.

In his advanced age he had a daughter named Guṇavatī. / Having no son, he gave his daughter to his disciple named Candra.

He regarded him as his own son, and he, self-controlled, regarded him like a father. / Once the two went to the forest seeking to gather kuśa grass and fuel.

They roamed here and there in a grove at the foot of the Himālaya mountains. / Then they saw a terrible rākṣasa approaching.

Their entire bodies trembling with terror, unable to flee, / they were slain by that rakṣas, who resembled Death himself.

Yet by the power of the sacred site and because of their virtuous nature, / they were taken to Vaikuṇṭha's abode by my attendants who remain near me.
Because of that worship of the Sun and other rites which they performed as long as they lived, / I was indeed exceedingly pleased with both of them by that deed.
Śaivas, Sauras, Gāṇeśas, Vaiṣṇavas, and Śakti-worshipers / reach me alone in this world, as rainwater reaches the ocean.
I, though one, have become fivefold, sporting under various names, / just as one Devadatta [is designated] by names for summoning sons and the like.

Then the two, dwelling in my abode, traveling in celestial chariots, both having the splendor of the sun, / possessing forms like mine and staying near me, enjoyed divine women, sandalwood, and delights.

6.89.m:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Then Guṇavatī, hearing that both had been slain by the rakṣas, / afflicted with grief caused by [the loss of] her father and husband, lamented piteously:

Guṇavatī said:
'O my lord! O father! Having abandoned me, where are you going without me? / I am a young woman; what shall I do today, truly destitute without you?
Who indeed will provide for me, staying at home, / miserable and unskilled in anything, with food, clothing, and the like out of affection?
Ill-fated, bereft of happiness, my protector gone, my life ruined— / to whose refuge shall I go today, since you were my protector, alas, immature as I am?'

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Thus having wailed much, severely distraught like an osprey, / she fell to the ground, devastated, like a plantain tree struck by the wind.
Regaining consciousness after a long time on the ground, having lamented much and piteously, / she remained plunged in the ocean of sorrow, tormented by grief.
Selling all her household utensils, doing good deeds, / she performed according to her ability the funeral rites for the next world for the two of them.
She took up residence in that very city for the rest of her life, / devoted to Viṣṇu, peaceful, truthful, pure, and self-restrained.
Two vows were duly observed by her from birth until death: / the vow of Ekādaśī and the proper observance of the month of Kārttika.
These two vows, O beloved, are exceedingly pleasing to me; / they grant worldly enjoyment and liberation, and bestow sons and prosperity.
Those who bathe at dawn every day in the month of Kārttika / when the sun is in Libra are liberated, even if they have committed great sins.
Men who sweep the temple of Viṣṇu, make offerings of svastika designs and the like, / and worship Viṣṇu are liberated while living.
Those men who practice bathing, keeping vigil, offering lamps, / and tending to the grove of tulasī in the month of Kārttika become embodiments of Viṣṇu.
Those who practice in this manner even for three days in the month of Kārttika / are to be revered even by the gods; how much more so those who have done it from birth?
Thus Guṇavatī properly spent every year, / ever devoted to the attendants of Viṣṇu, her mind fixed upon him.
Once, emaciated by old age and afflicted by fever, / she went somehow slowly to the Gaṅgā to bathe, O beloved.
As soon as she entered the water, trembling and tormented by cold, / distraught, she saw an aerial chariot arriving from the sky.
Approaching from the sky were [attendants] bearing conch, discus, mace, and lotus in hand, / fully bearing the form of Viṣṇu, marked with Garuḍa on their banners.
Placing her upon that celestial chariot attended by hosts of apsarases, / with fans waving over her, the attendants brought her to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, situated in that celestial chariot, resembling a blazing flame of fire, / through the merit of the Kārttika vow she attained my presence.
Then, in accordance with the entreaty of the gods headed by Brahmā, as I came / to the earth, all those attendants also came along with me.
All these Yādavas also are my very attendants, O lovely woman. / Your father, Devaśarman, became this king Satrājit;
and he who was Candraśarman is Akrūra; and you, O auspicious one, are that Guṇavatī / who greatly increased my love through the merit of the Kārttika vow.
Formerly a tulasī grove was made by you at my door; / therefore, O auspicious woman, this wish-granting tree stands in your courtyard.
And because lamps were offered by you formerly in Kārttika, / this Lakṣmī has become steadfast, residing in your body and home.
And because you dedicated all your vows and pious deeds to Viṣṇu in the form of your husband, / you have therefore come to be my wife.
Because of that vow which was performed in Kārttika formerly from birth until death, / you shall never experience separation from me.
Thus, those men who are devoted to vows in the month of Kārttika / have reached my presence, being granters of delight just as you are to me."
Men who perform sacrifices, gifts, vows, and austerities / truly do not attain even a fraction of the merit of the Kārttika vow.

Having heard this from the Lord of the world, feeling joy born from the glory of her virtuous previous birth, / Satyabhāmā bowed to Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the universe and sole primary cause of the three worlds, and spoke [these] words:

6.90.m: Satyabhāmā said: / All divisions of time are indeed portions of you whose nature is time, / and they are equal, O Lord; how then is Kārttika the best of months?
Among lunar days, the eleventh is dear [to you], and of months, Kārttika is dear. / Why is that so to you, O God of gods, Lord of lords? Tell me the reason!
The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / Well asked by you, O Satyā! Listen with single-pointed mind / to the conversation between Pṛthu, the son of Vena, and Nārada, the divine sage.
In this very way was Nārada questioned formerly by Pṛthu, my dear; / the all-knowing sage explained the reason for the preeminence of Kārttika.
Nārada said: / Formerly there was an Asura named Śaṅkha, a son of the ocean, / capable of tormenting the three worlds, possessed of great strength and valor.
Having defeated the gods and expelled them from the heavenly world, the great Asura / likewise seized the offices of the world-protectors, Indra and the others.
Then, out of fear of him, those gods went to a cave of the Golden Mountain; / accompanied by their women and led by Indra, they lived [there] for many years.
When the thirty [gods] were dwelling in the fortress of the Golden Mountain's cave / and had not come under his control, then the Daitya pondered:
"Although the thirty [gods] have been stripped of their authority and vanquished by me, / they still remain endowed with strength; what should be done by me in this matter?
Today it has been realized by me: the gods are endowed with the power of Vedic mantras; / I will carry them off, and then all of them will indeed become powerless."
Thinking thus, having observed Viṣṇu asleep, the demon, / the powerful lord, swiftly carried off the collection of the Vedas from the world of truth.
Carried off by him, the Vedas, however, escaped out of fear of him; / accompanied by the sacrificial mantras, they entered into the water here.
Searching for them, Śaṅkha also roamed within the ocean, / but the Daitya did not see them collected together anywhere.
Then Brahmā went together with the gods to take refuge in Viṣṇu; / taking articles of worship, he went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
There, to awaken him, the gods repeatedly performed rites / such as singing and playing instruments, offering perfumes, flowers, incenses, and lamps.
Then the Blessed One awakened, fully satisfied with their devotion, / and was seen there by those gods, possessing a radiance like a thousand suns.
Having worshiped [him] with the sixteen services, the thirty [gods] then / prostrated themselves like a staff upon the earth. Then Keśava spoke to them.
Viṣṇu said: / I am the giver of boons, O hosts of gods! By auspicious acts such as singing and playing instruments, / I grant to you all your heart's desires.
From the bright eleventh of the month of Āśvina until the awakening day [in Kārttika], / with the last fourth part of the night remaining, with auspicious songs, instruments, and the like,
whatever humans constantly perform, just as has been performed by you, / they constantly bring delight to me and indeed attain proximity to me.
Since that which was performed by you with foot-water, respectful offerings, sipping-water, and so forth / possessed wondrous excellence, it has become the cause of your happiness.
All the Vedas stolen by Śaṅkha are dwelling in the waters; / I shall slay that son of the ocean and bring them back, O gods.
From this day forward, let the Vedas, endowed with mantras, seed-syllables, and sacrifices, / rest every year in the waters constantly during the month of Kārttika.
From this day forward, I too shall dwell amidst the waters; / let you also, along with the lords of sages, come with me.
At this very time, the best among twice-born who perform the morning bath / become truly purified by the concluding ablutions of all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
Those men who properly and constantly perform the vow in Kārttika / are always to be led by you, O Śakra, to my abode at the end of their bodies.
By my command, you must provide protection for them against obstacles; / and by you, O Varuṇa, offspring such as sons and grandsons must be granted.
Increase of wealth, O lord of wealth [Kubera], must be effected by you at my command; / those men are visible bearers of my form and liberated while living.
And by those who have performed this highest vow from birth to death / according to the prescribed rule, they are worthy of respect even by you.
And since I was awakened by you on the eleventh [day], / therefore this lunar day is worthy of honor and always gives delight to me.
These two vows properly performed by men bestow proximity to Kṛṣṇa; there is no other. / Gifts, sacred bathing-places, austerities, and sacrifices bestow only the world of heaven, O best of gods!

6.99.m: Having thus fought a very brilliant battle, the radiant Viṣṇu / spoke to the king of the Daityas with a voice deep as a thundercloud:
And that mighty-armed Rāhu, with a voice deep as a thundercloud, / said to the god of the chiefs of gods: "Protect me who have come for refuge!
O Mahādeva, he has come near to devour me, a brāhmaṇa. / Protect me from him, O god of the chiefs of gods, affectionate to those seeking refuge!"
Hearing the words of the brāhmaṇa, Mahādeva then said: / "He must not be killed, since this messenger is dependent on another."
Hearing "Release him!", the being abandoned Rāhu in the sky. / Having released Rāhu, that being petitioned Mahādeva:
The being said: / "Hunger torments me, O Master, and I am emaciated with hunger in every way. / What shall be my food, O god of the chiefs of gods? Command me regarding that, O Lord!"
The Lord said: / "Quickly devour your own flesh of both hands and feet!"
Nārada said: / Commanded thus by Śiva, the being himself ate / the flesh arising from his hands and feet, so that only his head remained.
Seeing indeed that only his head remained, Sadāśiva, well-pleased / and full of wonder, spoke to that being of terrifying deeds:
The Lord said: / "You shall be known by the name Kīrtimukha, constantly stationed at my door. / Those who do not perform worship of you will never bring delight to me."
Nārada said: / From then on, Kīrtimukha remained at the door of the god. / If people do not worship him first here, their worship becomes useless.
Rāhu, released by him, fell into the Barbara country; / hence he attained fame on earth as "originating among the Barbaras".
And then, considering himself to be born anew in this [world], / Rāhu approached and told Jalandhara that entire deed of the Lord.
